headline: King Tides and leftover high surf bring moderate coastal flooding Friday morning during a warm, dry stretch, before a strong Pacific storm next Tuesday and Wednesday likely brings moderate to heavy rain from the coast to the mountains.

sections.title: Today & Tonight
sections.text: After a warm Thanksgiving with highs 10 to 15 degrees above normal, tonight stays clear to mostly clear along the coast and in the valleys, with only some thin high clouds. The northeast winds that blew earlier have weakened, and light offshore (land-to-sea) breezes continue overnight into Friday morning.

sections.title: Short Term
sections.text: Friday is the warmest day, with highs in the low to mid 80s at the coast, in the valleys and in the low deserts, low 60s to low 70s in the mountains and mid 60s to low 70s in the high desert; the light offshore breeze turns to an afternoon sea breeze. Over the weekend the high pressure overhead breaks down as a storm passes well to the north into the Pacific Northwest, so ocean breezes return and temperatures gradually cool Saturday and Sunday, though highs stay several degrees above normal. Expect some high clouds at times, with a chance of showers arriving Sunday night.

sections.title: Long Term
sections.text: Sunday night and Monday bring some subtropical moisture and roughly a 25 to 50 percent chance of showers from the mountains westward, but with little to set them off, amounts should be a tenth of an inch or less. A strong Pacific storm then moves through California Tuesday into Wednesday with gusty southwest to west winds and widespread rain; models disagree on how far south it digs, its timing, and how much moisture it carries (anywhere from too weak to count as an atmospheric river, a long stream of tropical moisture, to a moderate one), so rain totals are still uncertain. Current two-day estimates run about 1.5 to 3 inches from the mountains westward and 2.5 to 4 inches on the coastal mountain slopes, leaning toward a moderate to heavy rain event, with snow only above about 6,500 to 8,000 feet and a slight chance of thunderstorms, mainly from the coast into the valleys. Cooling spreads inland through midweek, and light showers could linger into Thursday (10 to 20 percent chance).

coast: A long-period west swell (7 to 9 feet every 16 to 18 seconds) is producing 6 to 8 foot breakers with local 10 to 12 foot sets on exposed west-facing beaches this evening, under a High Surf Advisory for San Diego County beaches until 4 AM Friday; surf lowers Friday morning to 3 to 5 feet, with sets to 7 feet on Saturday. Friday's 10 AM high tide is forecast around 7.6 to 7.7 feet, with tides running about a foot above normal predictions, so the King Tides plus surf bring moderate coastal flooding Friday morning under a Coastal Flood Warning for the Orange and San Diego County coasts until 1 PM Friday. Minor coastal flooding is possible Saturday morning where surf is elevated (high tide near 7 feet), with high tides falling below 7 feet Sunday. No hazardous boating conditions are expected through Monday, and thunderstorms are possible over the coastal waters with next Tuesday–Wednesday's storm.
watch_for: Moderate coastal flooding around Friday's 10 AM King Tide, under a Coastal Flood Warning until 1 PM Friday
Rain totals and timing for next Tuesday–Wednesday's storm, which could range from modest to a moderate atmospheric river
A slight chance of thunderstorms near the coast and valleys with that storm
confidence: Confidence is high in the warm, dry weather through the weekend; next Tuesday–Wednesday's storm is leaning toward moderate to heavy rain, but its track, timing and rain totals are still uncertain.
